title: The Comeback Arc
description: Six months ago, you led a product launch that failed spectacularly. The numbers were wrong, the timing was off, and you missed signals your team was trying to give you. You lost credibility, the team lost faith in you, and your own confidence took a serious hit. This is not a story about erasing that failure — it's about what you do next. Eight rounds. Eight real choices. The arc of recovery is rarely linear, but it is always possible.
learning_concept: Resilience is not a trait you either have or lack — it is a practiced skill built through how you interpret setbacks, manage your internal narrative, and take deliberate small actions over time.
learning_objectives: Understand the psychological stages of recovery from a professional failure and what makes each stage distinct
Recognize how perfectionism, self-blame, and avoidance patterns actively slow the recovery process
Practice reframing failure as information rather than identity, and distinguish healthy accountability from toxic shame
Build the capacity to take calibrated risks again after a confidence-damaging setback

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You play as a mid-level product leader recovering from a major career setback — a failed product launch you led six months ago
Each round presents a real scenario you'll face during your recovery: difficult conversations, internal doubts, new opportunities, and moments of testing
Choose one of three responses — each reflects a different mindset or strategy, and each has real costs and real benefits
Track your Confidence, Reputation, and Self-Trust as they shift with each decision — and watch how your psychological dimensions respond
The game is structured in three arcs: Rounds 1-3 (Accepting), Rounds 4-6 (Rebuilding), and Rounds 7-8 (Re-engaging) — each arc requires something different from you
tips: There is no perfect choice in this game — recovery is messy, and some rounds reward patience while others reward action
Pay attention to the coaching moments — they teach you how resilient people actually think differently about failure
Confidence is the hardest resource to rebuild because it requires genuine evidence, not just positive thinking
Your dimension scores reflect your psychological patterns — watch which ones are growing and which are holding you back
The most dangerous trap in recovery is performing recovery rather than doing it — the game is designed to surface that difference

psychological_framework.description: Recovery from professional failure engages multiple overlapping psychological systems. Resilience research (Bonanno, 2004; Ungar, 2012) shows that bouncing back is less about toughness and more about meaning-making — how we interpret what happened. The game draws on post-traumatic growth research, Carol Dweck's growth mindset framework, and the psychology of self-compassion (Neff, 2011) to show that how you talk to yourself in failure determines what you can build afterward.

core_skills.name: Resilience
core_skills.description: The capacity to absorb difficulty and adapt constructively — not the absence of pain, but the ability to keep moving while holding it

core_skills.name: Delayed Gratification
core_skills.description: Tolerating the discomfort of slow, incremental progress instead of reaching for quick fixes, external validation, or premature closure

core_skills.name: Risk Tolerance
core_skills.description: The willingness to act despite uncertainty — especially when a previous risk went badly and every instinct says to play it safe

core_skills.name: Adaptability
core_skills.description: The ability to update your beliefs, strategies, and self-image based on new evidence, rather than defending the past version of yourself

glossary_terms.definition: The psychological experience of a professional setback feeling like an attack on who you are, not just what you did
glossary_terms.example: Thinking 'I am a failure' instead of 'I failed at this particular thing' — the difference between a state and an identity
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research by Carol Dweck and others shows that people with fixed mindsets are more vulnerable to identity threat because they tie their self-worth to outcomes. People with growth mindsets can separate their actions from their identity, making recovery faster and more genuine.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Howard Schultz was forced out of Starbucks before returning to rebuild it into a global brand. He later described the period after his exit as one where he had to separate his ego from the company's identity — a crucial psychological step before he could return effectively.

glossary_terms.definition: Acting recovered — projecting confidence, signaling to others that you've moved on — while internally still stuck in shame, avoidance, or unprocessed grief
glossary_terms.example: Accepting a high-visibility project to prove you're fine when you haven't genuinely processed what went wrong — often leads to a second failure
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Performative recovery is particularly common in high-achievement cultures where showing vulnerability is punished. The cost is that it consumes enormous cognitive and emotional energy, leaving fewer resources for actual problem-solving. Research on emotional labor (Hochschild) shows that sustained performance of emotions you don't feel creates burnout.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Several Silicon Valley founders who faced high-profile product failures described the pressure to appear publicly confident while privately in crisis — those who did the genuine internal work first tended to build more durable second acts.

glossary_terms.definition: Taking risks that are sized appropriately to your current confidence level — not avoiding all risk, but not overcompensating either
glossary_terms.example: After a failed product launch, choosing to lead a smaller internal initiative before pitching to the board again — rebuilding evidence of competence in stages
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Psychologists distinguish between adaptive and maladaptive responses to failure. Avoidance (refusing all risk) and overcompensation (immediately swinging big to prove yourself) are both maladaptive. Calibrated risk-taking requires accurate self-assessment and the ability to tolerate incremental progress.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Athletes recovering from major injuries are taught not to return to full competition too early — the same principle applies professionally. Building back in stages creates genuine confidence rather than borrowed bravado.

halftime_config.reflection_question: You're halfway through your recovery arc. What has been harder than you expected — and what has surprised you about your own responses?
halftime_config.custom_message: The halfway point is often where the initial adrenaline of 'doing something about it' fades, and the actual slow work of rebuilding begins. This is where most people stall. Keep going.

rounds.title: The Monday Morning Reckoning
rounds.story: It has been six weeks since the launch failed. The post-mortem report sits in your inbox, unread. Your manager, Priya, has been generous — she hasn't pushed you out, but she's also quietly reassigned your three most senior direct reports to another team lead. You show up on Monday and two colleagues avoid eye contact in the corridor. You still have a job. You still have your title. But the air has changed, and you know it. Your calendar is half-empty in a way it never was before. Today Priya has asked you to come to a 1:1. You've been preparing for it like you're preparing for an interrogation.
rounds.goal: Decide how to show up to this conversation with your manager — and how honest you're willing to be about where you are.
rounds.coaching_moment: The instinct after failure is to project competence — to walk in there and perform 'I'm fine, I've learned, I'm ready.' But managers and leaders who have seen many recoveries can usually tell the difference between someone who has genuinely processed a setback and someone who is performing having processed it. Priya has been in this industry for 20 years. She probably can tell.

choices.label: Go in transparent — tell Priya exactly where you are, including the parts that aren't resolved yet
choices.feedback: You walked in and told Priya the truth: that the post-mortem report is still sitting in your inbox because you haven't been able to open it, that you know the team dynamic changed and you feel it, and that you're not sure yet what you want your next move to be. It was uncomfortable. Priya was quiet for a long moment. Then she said: 'That's the most honest thing anyone has said to me in a while.' She didn't have answers for you, but she stopped treating you like a liability and started treating you like a person. Reputation takes time to rebuild, but trust — real trust — sometimes starts with a single honest moment. You took a small but real step today.
choices.coaching_moment: Vulnerability in professional settings carries risk, but it also creates conditions for authentic support. Priya can only help you if she knows what you actually need.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You walked in and told Priya the truth: that the post-mortem report is still sitting in your inbox because you haven't been able to open it, that you know the team dynamic changed and you feel it, and that you're not sure yet what you want your next move to be. It was uncomfortable.

choices.label: Present a polished recovery plan — show Priya you've been working on what went wrong
choices.feedback: You came prepared: a slide deck with three key learnings, a revised process for future launches, and a proposed timeline for your return to full capacity. Priya seemed reassured — or at least, she had a framework to work with. But you notice something on the walk back to your desk: you feel more tired, not less. The work of preparing the deck distracted you from the deeper emotional processing you haven't done yet. The plan was good. Whether you believe it is a different question. Recovery built on performance rather than genuine reflection tends to surface the unresolved parts in the next setback.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You came prepared: a slide deck with three key learnings, a revised process for future launches, and a proposed timeline for your return to full capacity. Priya seemed reassured — or at least, she had a framework to work with.

choices.label: Ask Priya what she sees — let her perspective land before defending or explaining
choices.feedback: You opened the meeting differently than you planned. Instead of presenting or explaining, you said: 'Before I say anything, I'd like to hear what you're observing.' The question threw Priya off briefly — it's not what she expected. What she shared was both harder and more useful than any question you'd prepared for. She sees someone who is still in shock, avoiding the core issue, and at risk of retreating into execution tasks to avoid sitting with the discomfort of what happened. It stung. It was also accurate. You don't feel better leaving the room. But you feel clearer. Clarity, at this stage of recovery, is worth more than comfort.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What stories do you tell yourself on hard Monday mornings that help — and which ones make it worse?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Post-Mortem Report
rounds.story: You finally opened it. The post-mortem report is 34 pages and it is thorough. Your former lead engineer, Tanvir, clearly spent significant time on it. The document is professional and measured, but its findings are unambiguous: three key signals were deprioritized in the final three weeks before launch. In two of those cases, it was your call to deprioritize them. The third is ambiguous — you could reasonably argue it wasn't entirely your decision. The report has been shared across the product org. You know people have read it. Now you have to decide what to do with it.
rounds.goal: Determine how to respond to a formal post-mortem that places significant responsibility on your decisions — in a way that moves you and the organization forward.
rounds.coaching_moment: There's a psychological concept called 'defensive attribution' — the tendency to attribute failures to external factors and successes to internal ones. It's a cognitive protection mechanism, not a character flaw. The question is whether you're going to let it run unchecked or whether you're going to name the parts that were genuinely yours.

choices.label: Send an org-wide reply acknowledging the two decisions that were yours and what you'd do differently
choices.feedback: The reply took you three hours to write. It was two paragraphs. You acknowledged the two decisions clearly, named what you were optimizing for at the time, and described what you've learned about the trade-off you got wrong. You did not use passive voice, and you did not include qualifiers like 'to some extent' or 'in hindsight.' People noticed. Several colleagues who had been distant sent brief replies. Your former engineer Tanvir replied with just: 'This matters. Thank you.' Taking clear, unambiguous ownership of a mistake in a professional setting is rarer than it should be — and when it happens genuinely, it tends to shift how people see you more than a year of strong performance would.
choices.coaching_moment: Public accountability feels more dangerous than it usually is. Most people respond to genuine ownership with respect, not scorn.

choices.label: Schedule 1:1s with the key people affected — address it personally rather than publicly
choices.feedback: You reach out individually to Tanvir, to the two product managers who were affected, and to the lead designer. The conversations are harder than you anticipated — especially with Tanvir, who is more hurt than he let on in the report. But something shifts in each conversation. You're not managing the situation anymore; you're actually in it, with the people it affected. By the end of the week, three of the four conversations feel genuinely resolved — not because the failure was undone, but because you showed up for the relationship after the fall. The fourth — with one of the PMs — remains complicated. That's okay. Not everything resolves cleanly.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You reach out individually to Tanvir, to the two product managers who were affected, and to the lead designer. The conversations are harder than you anticipated — especially with Tanvir, who is more hurt than he let on in the report.

choices.label: Address the ambiguous third signal — make the case that it wasn't solely your responsibility
choices.feedback: You send a measured reply that addresses the two decisions but spends significant energy on the third — laying out the context, the stakeholders involved, and the fact that the report oversimplified the decision chain. Technically, you're not wrong. But in the culture of your organization, it reads as defensive. The two engineers who were most affected don't reply. Priya sends you a Slack: 'Can we talk?' Your reputation for the two things you did own partially recovers, but the energy you put into the third signal plants a new seed of doubt: does this person own their failures or just the ones they can't argue away? Recovery requires judgment about what to fight for. This wasn't that.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You send a measured reply that addresses the two decisions but spends significant energy on the third — laying out the context, the stakeholders involved, and the fact that the report oversimplified the decision chain. Technically, you're not wrong.

rounds.reflection_prompt: A post-mortem on yourself: what is the one honest thing you would put in the report about your own role in this?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Spiral at 2am
rounds.story: It's Tuesday at 2:17am and you're awake. This has been happening for weeks. Your mind runs the launch replay again — the sprint planning session where you overruled Tanvir, the board update where you said 'we're on track,' the launch day Slack channel going quiet. The narrative in your head has started to evolve from 'I made some bad calls' to something darker: maybe you were never actually good at this. Maybe the previous successes were luck. Maybe the people who stayed quiet at your launch meeting knew something you still don't know about yourself. This is the 2am version of you. It's not accurate, but it feels very real.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the middle-of-the-night spiral — one of the most reliable challenges of recovery from professional failure.
rounds.coaching_moment: Research by Kristin Neff on self-compassion shows that people who can interrupt the spiral with self-compassion recover faster and more durably than people who either (a) try to logic their way out, or (b) suppress the feelings. The key is to relate to yourself the way you'd relate to someone else you care about who was struggling.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the story you tell yourself about what the failure means about you — not just what happened, but what it says about who you are? Is that story accurate, or is it the 2am version?

choices.label: Write the spiral down — get it out of your head and on paper, without editing or defending yourself
choices.feedback: You open a notes app and write everything the 2am voice is saying — every accusation, every catastrophic interpretation, every 'maybe you were never good at this.' It takes 20 minutes and reads like a manifesto of self-attack. Then you do something simple: you read it back as if a friend had written it. Would you agree with these conclusions if a colleague showed you this list about themselves? Most of them: no. Some of them: maybe, but stated too harshly. One or two: worth sitting with. Writing the spiral down doesn't make it go away. But it does strip it of the authority that it has when it only exists inside your head.
choices.coaching_moment: Externalizing distress — getting it out of your head and into a form you can examine — is one of the most well-supported interventions in cognitive therapy. You don't need a therapist to use it.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You open a notes app and write everything the 2am voice is saying — every accusation, every catastrophic interpretation, every 'maybe you were never good at this. ' It takes 20 minutes and reads like a manifesto of self-attack.

choices.label: Do something concrete — organize your email, prep for tomorrow, get ahead of something
choices.feedback: You open your laptop and start clearing your inbox. By 4am, you've processed 47 emails and built a task list for the week. You feel more in control. When the alarm goes off at 7am, you feel the exhaustion — but also a fragile kind of productivity-buzz. The problem is that the feelings you were trying to outrun are still there, waiting. Activity is a legitimate coping mechanism, but at 2am it tends to be anxiety management rather than recovery work. The emails were fine. But what you actually needed was rest, and you traded it for the illusion of control.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You open your laptop and start clearing your inbox. By 4am, you've processed 47 emails and built a task list for the week.

choices.label: Call someone who has been through their own failure — not to fix it, just to not be alone with it
choices.feedback: You text your former colleague Samir — who left the company after his own difficult chapter two years ago and has since started something he's genuinely proud of. You say: 'Not good tonight. Can I call?' He picks up on the second ring. He doesn't fix anything. He doesn't tell you you'll be fine or that this was someone else's fault. He just says: 'I know this part. It gets less loud.' That's it. Something in the shared experience — being known by someone who has been in a similar place and survived — is qualitatively different from being comforted by someone who hasn't. You sleep eventually. The morning feels different.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The First Rebuild Move
rounds.story: You've been in a quieter role for eight weeks now. The spirals are less frequent. You've started actually reading the post-mortem document instead of just opening it and closing it again. Priya has given you a small project — overseeing the internal documentation system for the product team. It is not glamorous. Two years ago you would have seen this as a demotion. Today you're not sure how to see it. There's a version of you that wants to push back and ask for something bigger. There's another version that wonders if you're even ready for something bigger. You need to make a deliberate choice about how to show up for this work.
rounds.goal: Decide how to engage with a lower-visibility assignment during the rebuilding phase — and what that choice says about your relationship to your own ego.
rounds.coaching_moment: High achievers often have an inverse relationship between ego and recovery speed — the stronger the need to be seen as capable, the harder it is to do the quiet, competence-building work that actually rebuilds capability. The documentation project is genuinely useful. Whether it feels worthy is a different question.

choices.label: Do the documentation work well and find the genuine value in it — treat it as a real project, not a waiting room
choices.feedback: You spend three weeks actually interviewing the engineers and designers who use the documentation, mapping the gaps, and building something that solves the real problem instead of the surface problem. By the end, three teams are using it and one of the product managers who was hurt by the failed launch stops by and says: 'This is actually really useful.' It doesn't repair everything. But you notice something internal shift: you did something useful, clearly, without needing anyone to tell you it was a big deal. That's a kind of confidence that performance reviews don't create — it grows from evidence of genuine competence. Small as it was, it was real.

choices.label: Do the documentation work adequately but start making moves toward a more senior role — don't wait for permission to step back up
choices.feedback: The documentation gets done — adequately, not exceptionally. In parallel, you start positioning yourself for the product lead role opening in Q2, reaching out to stakeholders and making yourself visible in senior meetings. Some of it works. Priya notices your energy is split and mentions it. One of the senior PMs in the Q2 process asks for your documentation as a work sample — and its mixed quality gives you a harder interview than you expected. Recovery requires sequencing. Trying to skip the rebuilding phase to get back to the performing phase is a common trap, and this is its cost.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: The documentation gets done — adequately, not exceptionally. In parallel, you start positioning yourself for the product lead role opening in Q2, reaching out to stakeholders and making yourself visible in senior meetings.

choices.label: Go to Priya and tell her you're ready for something bigger — make the case directly
choices.feedback: You schedule time with Priya and make the case: that the documentation work is below your level, that you're ready to take on something meaningful, and that you're asking to be considered for the Q2 product lead role. Priya listens carefully. Then she says something you weren't ready for: 'I believe you believe you're ready. I'm not there yet. Let me be honest with you about why.' What follows is a 20-minute conversation about what she's still watching for. It's humbling — but it's also the most useful career feedback you've received in a year. Sometimes the move that feels like showing courage is actually showing impatience.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You schedule time with Priya and make the case: that the documentation work is below your level, that you're ready to take on something meaningful, and that you're asking to be considered for the Q2 product lead role. Priya listens carefully.

rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the smallest first step you can take right now — not the perfect step, just the first one?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: When Someone Else Gets the Role
rounds.story: The Q2 product lead role was announced this week. It went to Deepa — someone two years your junior, who joined the company after you. Deepa is talented. You know she is talented because you've worked with her. But there is something in your chest when you read the announcement that is more than professional disappointment. You find yourself analyzing what it means: is this permanent? Is Priya giving up on you? Is this what the rest of your time here looks like? The public-facing thing to do is congratulate Deepa. The private thing you're feeling is more complicated.
rounds.goal: Navigate the experience of a visible setback — someone else getting the role you wanted — without letting it derail your recovery arc.
rounds.coaching_moment: Comparative suffering — the experience of watching someone else's rise alongside your fall — is one of the hardest psychological tests in recovery. Research on social comparison theory shows that upward comparison to someone in your reference group is the most destabilizing form. What you do with that feeling determines whether it fuels you or corrodes you.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you compare yourself to where Deepa is right now, what do you feel? And under that feeling — what does it tell you about what you actually want?

choices.label: Congratulate Deepa genuinely, then take the day to feel what you feel without performing otherwise
choices.feedback: You send Deepa a brief, genuine message. Not gushing — just clear. 'Congrats. Well-earned.' Then you don't go to the team lunch. You take a long walk instead. You let yourself feel the complicated mix of sadness, envy, and something that might be relief that you didn't get it before you were ready. By evening, the sharpest edge has dulled. Deepa texts you: 'Thank you. I hope we work together on this.' You mean it when you say you hope so too. The ability to hold your own disappointment and someone else's success simultaneously without collapsing into resentment is a mark of real emotional maturity — and it pays dividends in the long run.

choices.label: Use it as fuel — treat this as the moment that clarifies what you need to do to get back
choices.feedback: The announcement becomes the thing that finally focuses you. You spend the week building a clear picture of what you would need to demonstrate to be considered for the next role at this level. You talk to two of the stakeholders in the hiring process and ask directly: 'What would change your assessment of me?' The answers are specific and useful. Two months from now, you're working on exactly the things they named. Motivation born from comparison can be powerful — but watch whether it's driving you toward something you genuinely want, or just away from something you're afraid of losing.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: The announcement becomes the thing that finally focuses you. You spend the week building a clear picture of what you would need to demonstrate to be considered for the next role at this level.

choices.label: Start exploring external opportunities — maybe this company is no longer the right place to rebuild
choices.feedback: You open your LinkedIn profile and start updating it. You reach out to two former colleagues who have moved to other companies. You're not panicking — you're exploring. And the act of exploring reminds you that you have options, which makes the current situation feel less like a trap. Within three weeks, you have two exploratory conversations. Neither leads anywhere immediately, but the act of doing it shifts something in how you show up internally — you're here because you're choosing to be, not because you have nowhere else to go. That's a different posture. Sometimes leaving is the right call; sometimes exploring the option is enough.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You open your LinkedIn profile and start updating it. You reach out to two former colleagues who have moved to other companies.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Mentor Who Got It Wrong
rounds.story: You've been meeting monthly with a mentor, Vikram — a VP at a different company who has known you for four years. Vikram was one of the people who first believed in your potential. This month, Vikram gives you advice that you suspect is wrong. He tells you to 'stop sitting on the sidelines' and push hard for a highly visible role on a new initiative — before you feel ready. 'The only way you get your reputation back is by taking big swings,' he says. Vikram means well. You also know, from the inside of your own experience, that this advice does not match where you actually are. But Vikram has been right before. And maybe you're just being cautious because you're afraid.
rounds.goal: Decide what to do when trusted advice conflicts with your own assessment of your readiness — one of the most subtle challenges in recovery.
rounds.coaching_moment: Well-meaning external advice can be one of the biggest sources of noise during recovery. People who care about you are often more impatient for your comeback than your actual readiness warrants. The skill here is calibration — distinguishing between advice that is genuinely useful versus advice that is more about the advisor's discomfort with your current state.

choices.label: Thank Vikram and decline — explain your own read on your readiness and commit to a different timeline
choices.feedback: You email Vikram a thoughtful reply: you appreciate the push, you've considered it seriously, and you've decided that the initiative he named isn't the right move right now — here's your thinking. Vikram replies: 'Interesting. You sound more certain than I've heard you sound in months.' That's not a coincidence. Self-trust is rebuilt in moments like this one — when you have external pressure to do something that doesn't feel right, and you choose your own assessment anyway. Not defensively, not stubbornly — but clearly. This is a different kind of confidence than the kind you had before the failure: it's less about performance and more about self-knowledge.

choices.label: Take a modified version — apply for the initiative but in a supporting role, not the lead
choices.feedback: You find a middle path: you reach out to the initiative lead and offer to contribute in a specific, bounded capacity — not leading the charge, but not sitting it out either. The initiative lead is glad to have you. The work is visible enough to start shifting perceptions, scoped enough that you're not overextended. Vikram is slightly disappointed you didn't go bigger, but he respects the move. By the end of the quarter, you have new evidence of your own competence — and it was earned, not borrowed. Sometimes the right answer is neither the advice you're given nor flat refusal, but a third option you design yourself.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You find a middle path: you reach out to the initiative lead and offer to contribute in a specific, bounded capacity — not leading the charge, but not sitting it out either. The initiative lead is glad to have you.

choices.label: Follow Vikram's advice — push for the lead role on the initiative and see what happens
choices.feedback: You apply for the lead role. You get it. For the first three weeks, you're running on adrenaline — it feels like being back. Then the workload hits a critical moment, and you feel your own foundations crack. You miss a key milestone. The quality of your thinking under pressure isn't where it was. You survive it — but you survive it barely, and the people watching can see the effort it's costing you. Vikram's advice was right about one thing: you needed visibility. But it was wrong about timing. Recovery at pace you can sustain almost always outperforms recovery at pace others think you should sustain.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You apply for the lead role. You get it.

rounds.reflection_prompt: When a mentor or advisor gets it wrong, what does that reveal about the limits of advice — and how do you still move forward?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The New Pitch
rounds.story: It's been five months since the failed launch. Something has quietly changed. Your documentation project has been cited as a model in two team retrospectives. The exploratory conversations you had outside the company made you realize you actually want to stay — not out of inertia, but because you believe in the product direction. Priya has started including you in senior planning conversations again. And now there is an opportunity: a mid-size new initiative needs a lead, and Priya has told you — with some specificity — that you're being considered. But you have to pitch for it. You have to stand in front of a panel and make the case. The last time you stood in front of a panel with high stakes, it was the launch presentation that preceded the failure.
rounds.goal: Prepare for and decide how to approach a high-stakes pitch that will test whether your rebuilt confidence is real or still fragile.
rounds.coaching_moment: This is the moment the recovery arc has been building toward — not a triumphant return, but a genuine test. The most important thing is not to perform confidence. The most important thing is to walk in knowing what you know, knowing what you don't know, and being willing to name both.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Before you go into this pitch — what do you actually believe about yourself now, versus what you believed about yourself before the failure? What is different? What is the same?

choices.label: Structure the pitch around what you learned from the failed launch — make the failure part of your case for why you're ready
choices.feedback: The pitch opens with a line that the room didn't expect: 'The last time I stood in front of a group like this, I told you I was confident and I was wrong. I'm not going to tell you I'm confident today — I'm going to tell you what I know about this problem, what I don't know, and how I plan to work in the spaces in between.' The room shifts. The questions that follow are harder than you've had in a while, and you answer most of them well. One you don't know. You say so directly. Priya tells you later that the panel's feedback was unanimous: 'We want someone who has been through something.' You have been. It shows.
choices.coaching_moment: This kind of pitch is rare and powerful because it's true. The failure, owned and processed, becomes an asset — a different kind of credibility than someone who has never been tested.

choices.label: Pitch forward — focus entirely on the opportunity, the plan, and the execution approach, not the past
choices.feedback: You deliver a clean, forward-focused pitch. You've done your research, your execution plan is specific, and you answer the questions well. The panel is impressed. Priya tells you it was strong. Afterward, one of the panel members — a VP who knew about the failed launch — pulls you aside and says: 'Good pitch. One thing I'd push on: how did the last one make you different?' It's a soft question. You give a decent answer. But you leave knowing there was a version of that pitch that would have been more powerful — and you know what it was.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You deliver a clean, forward-focused pitch. You've done your research, your execution plan is specific, and you answer the questions well.

choices.label: Ask for a preliminary conversation with Priya before pitching — make sure you're aligned on what they're looking for first

Priya respects the ask and gives you specific guidance. Your pitch is sharper as a result — targeted to the actual concerns rather than what you imagined they'd be. The panel notices that you asked for input and used it well. rounds.title: You Got It. Now What?
rounds.story: You got the role. Priya called you on a Thursday afternoon, and you sat with it for a full minute before you said anything. The new initiative starts in three weeks. You're already getting emails from the team, calendar invites are populating, and people are starting to look to you again. There is a version of you that wants to immediately prove — to Priya, to the team, to the people who doubted you, and honestly to yourself — that you're back and that the failure was a blip. You know where that version leads. The question is: what kind of leader are you going to be in this next chapter?
rounds.goal: Decide how to begin the next chapter — not just how to perform a comeback, but how to lead differently based on what you learned.
rounds.coaching_moment: The real test of a recovery arc isn't whether you get back — it's what you bring back with you. The people who recover most durably are not those who return to exactly who they were before. They're the ones who carry something from the experience — genuine knowledge about themselves, their limits, and their patterns — that makes them different leaders.

choices.label: Meet individually with every person on the new team before making any structural or process decisions
choices.feedback: You spend the first two weeks doing nothing but listening. No announcements, no reorgs, no big visible moves. Just individual conversations with each member of the team. You ask what they know, what they worry about, what they've seen leaders miss. Two conversations reveal concerns about scope you hadn't factored into your plan. One reveals a technical dependency that would have caused a delay six weeks in. You adjust before you even start. The team notices that you asked before you acted. That's not the leader you were before the failure. It's a better one. The arc isn't over — but this is what growth actually looks like: not returning to who you were, but becoming someone sharper.
choices.coaching_moment: The failure taught you that signals you dismissed came back to cost you. The best leaders build systems that make it hard to dismiss signals — starting with listening before deciding.

choices.label: Set a clear 30-60-90 plan and communicate it to the team on day one — show them you're decisive and prepared
choices.feedback: Your day-one communication is clear, structured, and well-received. The team knows what to expect and feels like they have a leader. One engineer tells you: 'This is helpful. The last lead just winged it.' You're delivering on the basics. The risk is subtle: the 30-60-90 plan was built with external data, not internal knowledge. Three months in, one of your assumptions turns out to be wrong — not catastrophically, but enough that you have to adjust publicly. The team handles it fine. You handle it better than you would have before. You've learned something about adjusting without making it a crisis. That's real progress.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Your day-one communication is clear, structured, and well-received. The team knows what to expect and feels like they have a leader.

choices.label: Be explicit with the team about what you learned from the failed launch and how you're leading differently
choices.feedback: In your first team meeting, you say something unusual: 'Some of you may know I led a launch last year that didn't go well. I want to be upfront about what I learned from it, because it directly shapes how I'm going to lead here.' You tell them: you deprioritized signals you didn't want to hear. You overconfidently projected timelines without enough uncertainty. You're going to run this initiative differently — here's how. The room is quiet for a moment. Then your lead engineer says: 'That's honest. I'm in.' It's not a triumphant comeback speech. It's something better: a leader who has been somewhere hard and came back with something real to show for it. That's the arc.

transfer_exercises.real_world: After any professional setback, the most important act of accountability is to name clearly — to yourself and relevant others — what decisions were yours, without qualification or deflection
transfer_exercises.challenge: Think of a recent situation where you made a mistake. Write two sentences: one that clearly names what you did, and one that names what you would do differently. Share it with one person who was affected.

transfer_exercises.game_context: In Round 4, you had to decide whether to do a lower-visibility assignment excellently or chase the more senior role too soon
transfer_exercises.real_world: Recovery from professional setbacks almost always requires a period of doing smaller things very well before larger opportunities become available again. The instinct to skip that phase is almost always wrong.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Identify one assignment or task you are currently undervaluing because it feels beneath you. Spend one week treating it as your most important project and see what you learn from it.
